extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent prosecutors, and their attorneys (practitioners litigating/petitioning before the USPTO)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when and how to petition the Director under 37 CFR 1.181, and related standards for Office actions, replies, evidence, and appeals during patent examination and prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of an Office action under 35 U.S.C. § 132
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 132 ensures that an applicant 'at least be informed of the broad statutory basis for [the rejection of] his claims, so that he may determine what the issues are on which he can or should produce evidence.' Section 132 is violated when a rejection is so uninformative that it prevents the applicant from recognizing and seeking to counter the grounds for rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An Office action must provide enough information specific to the application to place the applicant on notice of the basis for rejections so the applicant can recognize and counter them. The mere inclusion of boilerplate language does not render an Office action insufficient if it still contains enough application‑specific information. (Cites Chester v. Miller and MPEP references.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and acceptability of boilerplate/template language in Office actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP) contains numerous template form paragraphs for use by examiners (and which examiners are expected to use). The mere inclusion of 'boilerplate' information in an Office action does not render an Office action in violation of 35 U.S.C. § 132.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An Office action typically contains template passages and unique information; what matters is whether there is sufficient application‑specific content to inform the applicant of the grounds for rejection. Differences of opinion about scope or adequacy are typical and not by themselves a basis for a 1.181 petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reply requirements under 37 CFR 1.111(b) — specificity and completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The reply must 'distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the examiner's action and must reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the prior Office action.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replies must present arguments pointing out the specific distinctions believed to render the claims patentable over applied references. A general allegation that the claims define a patentable invention without specific explanation does not comply. The reply must appear to be a bona fide attempt to advance the application. Matters challenging examiner reliability/pertinence are appropriate in a 1.111 reply, not via 1.181 petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on supplemental replies (37 CFR 1.111(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: A reply that is supplemental to a compliant reply will not be entered as a matter of right except as provided; the Office may enter a supplemental reply only if clearly limited to certain categories (e.g., cancellation of claims, adoption of examiner suggestions, placing application in condition for allowance, reply to an Office requirement made after the first reply, correction of informalities, or simplification of issues for appeal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A supplemental reply will be entered if filed during a period when Office action is suspended under §1.103(a) or (c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment requirements in reply to a rejection (37 CFR 1.111(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: When amending in reply to a rejection, the applicant must 'clearly point out the patentable novelty which he or she thinks the claims present in view of the state of the art disclosed by the references cited or the objections made' and show how the amendments avoid such references or objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments must make it clear how the changed claim language overcomes the cited art/objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence to traverse rejections must be by oath/declaration (37 CFR 1.132)
rubrics_metrics.description: When any claim is rejected or objected to, any evidence submitted to traverse the rejection or objection on a basis not otherwise provided for must be by way of an oath or declaration under this section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantive evidence offered to rebut examiner factual assumptions should be provided in the form required by 1.132 (oath/declaration) where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: What may be petitioned to the Director under 37 CFR 1.181
rubrics_metrics.description: Petition may be taken to the Director from any action or requirement of any examiner in ex parte prosecution (or certain reexamination) not subject to appeal to the PTAB; in cases where statute or rules specify review by the Director; and to invoke the Director's supervisory authority in appropriate circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitions under 1.181 are for limited circumstances; they are not a substitute for appeals of examiners' rejections that are reviewable by the Board. The Director will not ordinarily entertain petitions that usurp the Board's appellate functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on Director's supervisory role and petitions (not to usurp PTAB jurisdiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director 'will not, on petition, usurp the functions or impinge upon the jurisdiction of the Patent Trial and Appeal Board.' Adverse examiner decisions reviewable by the Board are those related to the rejection of claims, and petition is not ordinarily appropriate where the question is appealable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants dissatisfied with an examiner's rejection should use appeal under 35 U.S.C. § 134 and 37 CFR 41.31 when appropriate. Petitions should not be used to resolve issues that are properly appealable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal rights and procedures under 35 U.S.C. § 134 and 37 CFR 41.31
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant whose claims have been twice rejected may appeal to the Patent Trial and Appeal Board by filing a notice of appeal with the required fee within the time period for reply. An appeal is presumed to be taken from the rejection of all claims under rejection unless cancelled by amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Who may appeal, timing, signature exceptions, and extendability of time periods (under §1.136 or §1.550(c)) are governed by 41.31. Questions not affecting merits may be required to be settled before the appeal can be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standards in USPTO proceedings — FRE/Daubert not applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Rules of Evidence (and Daubert gatekeeping) are not applicable in proceedings before administrative agencies or specifically before the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments that evidence would be inadmissible in court (e.g., Daubert) are immaterial to USPTO examination; admissibility and weight are matters for the decision maker (examiner) and can be addressed in reply or on appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance and admission of evidence in agency proceedings (5 U.S.C. § 553(d)/§556(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: While agencies should provide for exclusion of irrelevant, immaterial, or unduly repetitious evidence, courts recognize that agency decision makers are competent to disregard or discount evidence and may err on the side of inclusion to facilitate efficient fact‑finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence need not prove the exact point for which it is proffered to be relevant. Inclusion/exclusion rulings are not the usual function of the Director via 1.181 petitions; disputes over evidentiary weight should be made to the examiner in reply or on appeal. Case law cited indicates agencies tend to allow relevant evidence and weigh it rather than rigidly exclude it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of production and persuasion in examination
rubrics_metrics.description: The burdens of production and of persuasion applicable during the patent examination process are set by Federal Circuit case law and MPEP, and are not affected by the inclusion of particular discussion in an Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusion of argumentative or evidentiary discussion in an Office action does not shift the legal burdens; applicants must still rebut the examiner's prima facie case through argument and/or evidence per established standards (e.g., MPEP §2107.02 and cited Federal Circuit cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality initiatives do not create new bases for petition relief
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO quality initiatives (e.g., EPQI, Patents Ombudsman Program) do not create any basis for relief via petition under 37 CFR 1.181 that does not already exist under statutes, regulations, and examining procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs like the Patents Ombudsman cannot be used as an alternative forum to resolve disagreements that are currently resolved via appeal, petition, or other procedures; failure of personnel to follow USPTO guidance materials is not by itself a proper basis for appeal or petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process / notice and opportunity to rebut in examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice in an Office action of the reasons and evidence for rejection, together with the applicant's right to rebut and present evidence to challenge those statements and evidence, satisfies constitutional due process requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may challenge examiner evidence and reasoning by argument and/or by submitting evidence (including oaths/declarations where required) in a 1.111 reply or on appeal; the Office action must place the applicant on notice of the basis for the rejection.
